opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changed things quite a lot, honestly. Before ChatGPT, when you talked to clinicians about AI, it felt fairly abstract. It was something happening in research papers, or a model that read retinal scans or flagged something on a chest X-ray. Many doctors were skeptical, and reasonably so. They'd seen a lot of hype, and many tools didn't fit into how they actually worked.

What ChatGPT did was put a capable system directly in people's hands. Doctors could try it themselves, at home, on their own questions. They could ask it to summarize a paper, draft a letter to an insurer, or explain a condition in plain language for a patient. That hands-on experience did more to shift attitudes than years of conference talks. Suddenly it wasn't "AI might help someday." It was "I used this last night and it saved me twenty minutes."

It also changed what people imagine AI is for. Earlier medical AI was mostly narrow: one model, one task, one image type. Large language models made people realize AI could help with the enormous amount of text and administrative work in medicine, like documentation, notes, and correspondence. That's where much of physician burnout comes from, so the appeal was immediate.

That said, I'd add a caution. More willingness doesn't automatically mean appropriate use. These models can still be confidently wrong, and in medicine that matters enormously. So the conversation has moved from "should we use AI at all?" to "how do we use it safely, how do we evaluate it, and where does a human need to stay firmly in the loop?" That's a much healthier conversation, but it's one where the field still has a lot of work to do.

r001.rationale: The response says doctors’ personal experience with ChatGPT shifted attitudes, but does not say widespread use creates social pressure for doctors to use AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses hands-on experience and cautions that models can be wrong, but does not say ChatGPT makes AI feel less dangerous to doctors.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think ChatGPT did more for physician adoption of AI in about six months than the whole field managed in the previous ten years, and not really because of anything technical. It changed the social contract around the technology.

Before ChatGPT, when you went to a clinician and said "we have an AI model," what they heard was "a black box some engineer built that's going to tell me I'm wrong and that I can't argue with." It was a product being done to them. Every pitch was a risk score popping up in the EHR, another alert in a system that was already drowning them in alerts. So the natural response was skepticism, and frankly it was a healthy skepticism.

What ChatGPT did was put the thing directly in their hands, with no IT department and no vendor in the middle. Doctors went home, opened a browser, and started typing in the questions they actually have: summarize these guidelines, draft this prior auth letter, explain this to a patient at a fifth-grade reading level. And they could see it reason in language, push back on it, catch it being wrong. That tactile experience is completely different from being handed a probability. You develop an intuition for where it's good and where it's dangerous, the same way you do with a new resident.

The second thing is that it attacked the right problem first. For years the field was obsessed with diagnosis, which is the part of the job doctors are actually proud of and don't want to give away. The pain was always the paperwork. The inbox, the notes, the fact that you spend two hours on documentation for every hour with patients. Large language models happened to be good at exactly that, so the first encounter was with something that gave time back rather than something that second-guessed judgment. Ambient scribing is the clearest example. I've talked to clinicians who were deeply anti-AI two years ago who now say they would quit if you took the scribe away.

Now, I want to be careful. Willingness to use is not the same as appropriate use. There's a real hallucination problem, there's the issue of people pasting patient data into consumer tools, and the enthusiasm has in some places gotten ahead of the evidence. The thing I watch for is whether the trust is calibrated. The good news is that because doctors learned this technology by playing with it, a lot of them have a better instinct for its failure modes than the people selling it to them. That's a much healthier starting point than where we were.

r001.rationale: The response says hands-on ChatGPT use increased doctors’ willingness and changed the social contract, but it does not say widespread use creates social pressure for doctors to use AI.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AI as a black box imposed on clinicians with direct use that lets doctors test it, challenge it, and learn its failure modes, describing this as a healthier starting point. This communicates that AI feels less threatening to doctors.

astra-6.text:
I think ChatGPT has made doctors much more willing to try AI because they can interact with it directly. You don’t need a technical background to ask it a question, give it some text to summarize, or see whether it can help draft something. That makes the potential much more tangible.

But being willing to try it is different from trusting it in patient care. It can give a very convincing answer that’s wrong, and a doctor needs to understand those limitations. So I think it’s opened the door, particularly for things like documentation and administrative work. Using it to support clinical decisions still requires careful validation and oversight.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT makes doctors more willing to try AI because they can interact with it directly. It does not say widespread use creates social pressure to use AI.

r002.rationale: The response says AI’s potential feels more tangible, but does not say ChatGPT makes AI feel less dangerous to doctors. It instead cautions that AI can give convincing but wrong answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ChatGPT has made AI feel much more tangible to doctors. You can interact with it in plain language, ask follow-up questions, and quickly see how it might help with something you do every day. That lowers the barrier to trying it.

But willingness to try AI is different from trusting it with a clinical decision. A doctor might be comfortable using it to draft a note or explain a concept, while wanting much stronger evidence before relying on it for diagnosis or treatment. So I think the biggest change is that more doctors are asking, “Where could this be useful?” And then the next questions are: How reliable is it, how do I check its work, and does it actually help me care for patients?
